Fast Facts

  • Flip the inequality sign whenever multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
  • Same slope + different intercept = no solution. Same slope + same intercept = infinite solutions.
  • A sum of squares (a² + b²) does NOT factor over the real numbers — only a difference does.
  • Always check radical-equation solutions in the ORIGINAL equation for extraneous answers.
  • Correlation does not imply causation — a lurking third variable can explain both.
  • Check units in your final answer before moving on.
memoryHtml:
Quick ways to lock in the facts you keep forgetting. Read the big trick, then the small note tells you what it unlocks. Say them out loud — silly is memorable.

Equations & Inequalities

Flip it for negatives
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number flips the sign. Nothing else in algebra flips a sign like this — it's the #1 inequality trap.
True = infinite, false = none
If solving an equation leaves a TRUE statement (5=5), every x works (infinite solutions). If it leaves a FALSE statement (5=8), no x works (no solution).
Absolute value splits in two
|x| = a always means x = a OR x = −a. Distance from zero can go either direction.

Linear Functions

Rise over run, not run over rise
Slope = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). The y's go on top. Mixing up the order flips the sign of the slope.
Parallel = same, perpendicular = flip-and-negate
Parallel lines share the exact same slope. Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other (2 and −½).
Vertical is UNdefined, horizontal is ZERO
A vertical line (x = #) has undefined slope. A horizontal line (y = #) has zero slope. Easy to swap under pressure — say them together to lock the pairing in.

Systems

Same slope decides everything
Different slopes → one solution. Same slope, different intercept → parallel, no solution. Same slope AND intercept → the same line, infinite solutions.
Test a point to know which way to shade
When graphing an inequality, plug a test point (often the origin) into the ORIGINAL inequality. If it's true, shade that side.

Exponents & Polynomials

Same base: add to multiply, subtract to divide
xᵃ·xᵇ = x^(a+b) when multiplying; xᵃ/xᵇ = x^(a−b) when dividing. A power of a power MULTIPLIES the exponents instead.
Anything to the zero is one
x⁰ = 1 for any nonzero base — a trap answer people second-guess.
FOIL: First, Outer, Inner, Last
The order for multiplying two binomials, so you never miss a term.

Factoring

GCF first, always
Before trying any other factoring method, check for a greatest common factor — it makes every later step smaller and easier.
Squares subtract, they don't add
a² − b² factors neatly into (a+b)(a−b). a² + b² does NOT factor over the real numbers — there's no pattern for a sum of squares.

Quadratics

Zero first, then factor
The Zero Product Property only works when one side of the equation is 0 — always move everything over before factoring and solving.
Discriminant sign tells the story
Positive discriminant → two real solutions. Zero → exactly one. Negative → none. No need to finish solving just to count solutions.

Radicals

Only like radicals combine
3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2, but √2 + √3 cannot be combined — the number under the root has to match, just like combining like terms.
Squaring can lie to you
Always plug your answer back into the ORIGINAL radical equation. Squaring both sides can create a fake (extraneous) solution that doesn't actually work.

Exponential Functions & Sequences

Add for arithmetic, multiply for geometric
Arithmetic sequences ADD a common difference between terms. Geometric sequences MULTIPLY by a common ratio. Check which operation connects the terms.
Exponential always wins eventually
No matter how big a linear function's starting advantage is, exponential growth eventually overtakes it given enough time.

Statistics

Mean chases the tail
In a right-skewed distribution, the mean is pulled higher than the median (toward the tail). In a left-skewed distribution, it's pulled lower.
Correlation isn't causation
A strong r value just means two variables move together — it never proves one causes the other. Look for a hidden third variable.

Functions

f(x) is a label, not multiplication
f(x) means "the output of f when the input is x," not f times x. Read it as a whole phrase, not two separate pieces.
Horizontal shifts feel backwards
f(x − 3) shifts the graph RIGHT, not left. Vertical shifts feel normal: f(x) − 3 shifts DOWN. When in doubt, plug in a test value and check.

units.name: Solving Equations & Inequalities

concepts.intro: Every equation is a balance — whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. The goal is always to isolate the variable.
b: Combine like terms on each side first, then use inverse operations (undo addition/subtraction, then multiplication/division) to isolate the variable.
Distribute before combining like terms: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12, not 3x + 4.
An equation with the SAME variable term on both sides that cancels out to a TRUE statement (like 5 = 5) has infinite solutions.
An equation that cancels out to a FALSE statement (like 5 = 8) has no solution.

concepts.intro: A literal equation has more than one variable — you solve for ONE of them in terms of the others, using the exact same steps as any other equation.
b: Treat every other variable as if it were a number — isolate the target variable using inverse operations.
Example: solve A = ½bh for h → multiply both sides by 2, then divide by b → h = 2A/b.
Common formulas to practice on: perimeter, simple interest I = Prt, temperature conversion.

concepts.intro: Inequalities solve almost exactly like equations, with one critical rule that trips people up constantly.
b: Flip the inequality symbol whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a NEGATIVE number.
Graph on a number line: open circle for < or >, closed (filled) circle for ≤ or ≥. Shade the direction the inequality points.
Compound inequalities like −3 < x ≤ 5 mean x is between −3 (exclusive) and 5 (inclusive) — graph both boundaries.

concepts.intro: Absolute value measures distance from zero, so it always splits into two cases.
b: |x| = a (a > 0) means x = a OR x = −a. Solve both.
|x| < a means −a < x < a (a compound 'between' inequality).
|x| > a means x < −a OR x > a (two separate rays going outward).

traps: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative is the #1 error on this unit.
Distributing a negative: −2(x − 5) = −2x + 10, NOT −2x − 10. Watch the sign on the second term.
|x| < a and |x| > a graph completely differently — one is a segment between two points, the other is two separate rays.
fms: Solve: isolate the variable using inverse operations, in reverse PEMDAS order
Flip inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative
|x| = a → x = a or x = −a (a > 0)

units.name: Linear Functions & Graphing

concepts.intro: Slope measures steepness — how much y changes for every step in x.
b: Slope formula: m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁), often remembered as 'rise over run.'
Positive slope rises left to right; negative slope falls left to right.
A horizontal line has slope 0 (y = constant). A vertical line has UNDEFINED slope (x = constant) — you cannot divide by zero.

concepts.intro: The same line can be written three different ways — pick whichever form fits the information you're given.
b: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b (m = slope, b = y-intercept). Best for graphing quickly.
Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Best when you have a point and a slope.
Standard form: Ax + By = C. Useful for finding intercepts quickly (set x = 0 for the y-intercept, y = 0 for the x-intercept).

concepts.intro: Most problems give you two pieces of information and ask for the equation.
b: Given two points: find slope first with the slope formula, then plug one point into point-slope form.
Parallel lines have the SAME slope.
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are NEGATIVE RECIPROCALS (they multiply to −1). Example: 2 and −½.

concepts.intro: Intercepts are where a line crosses each axis — fast, reliable points for graphing.
b: x-intercept: set y = 0 and solve for x (where the line crosses the x-axis).
y-intercept: set x = 0 and solve for y (where the line crosses the y-axis) — this is the 'b' in y = mx + b.
Two points (like the two intercepts) are all you need to graph any line.

traps: Slope formula order matters for the SIGN of individual differences, but as long as you keep y's and x's in the same point-order in numerator and denominator, the slope comes out the same either way.
Vertical lines (x = #) have UNDEFINED slope; horizontal lines (y = #) have ZERO slope — these are opposite and commonly swapped.
Perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, not just the negative. For 2/3 it's −3/2, not −2/3.
fms: Slope: m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁)
Slope-intercept: y = mx + b · Point-slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Parallel: same slope · Perpendicular: negative reciprocal slopes

units.name: Systems of Equations & Inequalities

concepts.intro: Substitution works best when one equation is already solved for a variable (or easy to solve).
b: Solve one equation for one variable, then substitute that expression into the OTHER equation.
Solve the resulting one-variable equation, then plug that value back in to find the second variable.
Always write your answer as an ordered pair (x, y).

concepts.intro: Elimination works by adding or subtracting the equations to cancel out one variable.
b: Line up the equations, then multiply one or both by a constant so one variable's coefficients are opposites.
Add the equations to eliminate that variable, solve for what's left, then back-substitute.
Elimination is fastest when both equations are already in standard form (Ax + By = C).

concepts.intro: Two lines can relate to each other in exactly three ways.
b: Different slopes → lines cross once → ONE solution (the normal case).
Same slope, different y-intercept → parallel lines → NO solution.
Same slope AND same y-intercept → the same line → INFINITE solutions.

concepts.intro: Graphing a system of inequalities means finding the region where BOTH shaded areas overlap.
b: Graph each inequality's boundary line (dashed for < or >, solid for ≤ or ≥) and shade its solution side.
The solution to the SYSTEM is only the region where both shadings overlap.
Test a point (often the origin, if not on a line) in the ORIGINAL inequality to check which side to shade.

traps: Solving a system algebraically but forgetting to give BOTH coordinates of the answer — a system's solution is a point (x, y), not just a single number.
Dashed boundary lines mean the line itself is NOT included (< or >); solid lines mean it IS included (≤ or ≥).
When a system has no solution, students often think they made an error — but 0 = 8 (a false, variable-free statement) correctly means 'no solution,' not a mistake.
fms: Substitution: solve for one variable, plug into the other equation
Elimination: add/subtract equations to cancel a variable
Same slope + different intercept = no solution · Same slope + same intercept = infinite solutions

units.name: Exponents & Polynomials

concepts.intro: These rules let you simplify expressions with exponents without ever expanding them out.
b: Product rule: xᵃ · xᵇ = x^(a+b) — multiplying same bases, ADD the exponents.
Quotient rule: xᵃ / xᵇ = x^(a−b) — dividing same bases, SUBTRACT the exponents.
Power rule: (xᵃ)ᵇ = x^(ab) — a power raised to a power, MULTIPLY the exponents.
Zero exponent: x⁰ = 1 (any nonzero base). Negative exponent: x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ (flip to the denominator).

concepts.intro: A polynomial is a sum of terms with whole-number exponents on the variable.
b: Monomial: one term (5x²). Binomial: two terms (x + 3). Trinomial: three terms (x² + 2x − 1).
The degree of a polynomial is the HIGHEST exponent present. A degree-2 polynomial is 'quadratic'; degree-1 is 'linear.'
Like terms have the exact same variable AND exponent (3x² and −5x² are like terms; 3x² and 3x are not).

concepts.intro: Combine only like terms — everything else stays as it is.
b: Line up like terms and add/subtract their coefficients.
When subtracting a polynomial, distribute the negative sign to EVERY term inside the parentheses first.
Example: (3x² + 2x) − (x² − 5x) = 3x² + 2x − x² + 5x = 2x² + 7x.

concepts.intro: Every term in the first polynomial must multiply every term in the second.
b: Monomial × polynomial: distribute the monomial to every term.
Binomial × binomial: use FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last), then combine like terms.
Binomial × trinomial: distribute each term of the binomial across all three terms of the trinomial, then combine like terms.

traps: x⁰ = 1, NOT 0 — a very common trap answer.
When subtracting polynomials, forgetting to distribute the negative to EVERY term in the second polynomial, not just the first.
(x + 3)² is NOT x² + 9 — you must FOIL it out: (x+3)(x+3) = x² + 6x + 9.
fms: xᵃ·xᵇ = x^(a+b) · xᵃ/xᵇ = x^(a−b) · (xᵃ)ᵇ = x^(ab)
x⁰ = 1 · x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ
FOIL: First, Outer, Inner, Last

units.name: Factoring

concepts.intro: Always check for a GCF FIRST, before trying any other factoring method.
b: Find the largest number and variable power common to every term, then pull it out front.
Example: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3) — 3x is the GCF of 6x² and 9x.
Factoring is the reverse of distributing — you can always check by multiplying back out.

concepts.intro: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
b: x² + 7x + 12: need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7 → 3 and 4 → (x + 3)(x + 4).
If c is positive and b is positive, both factors are positive. If c is positive and b is negative, both factors are negative.
If c is negative, the two factors have opposite signs (one positive, one negative).

concepts.intro: Two patterns show up constantly and can be factored instantly once recognized.
b: Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). There is NO middle term.
There is no such pattern for a SUM of squares (a² + b²) — it does not factor over the reals.
Perfect square trinomial: a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)². Recognize by checking if the first and last terms are perfect squares.

concepts.intro: Used for four-term polynomials or trinomials where a ≠ 1.
b: Split the middle term(s) so you can group the polynomial into two pairs, each with its own GCF.
Factor the GCF out of each pair — if done correctly, both pairs share the same leftover binomial.
Factor that common binomial out one final time.

traps: Always check for a GCF first — trying to factor 4x² + 8x + 4 as a trinomial directly is much harder than pulling out the GCF of 4 first: 4(x² + 2x + 1) = 4(x+1)².
a² − b² factors, but a² + b² does NOT factor (over the real numbers) — a very common trap.
Signs matter: c positive & b positive → both factors positive; c negative → factors have opposite signs.
fms: GCF: pull out the largest shared factor first
a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b)
x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c, add to b

units.name: Quadratic Equations & Functions

concepts.intro: The Zero Product Property is the engine behind solving quadratics by factoring.
b: Set the equation equal to 0 first (move everything to one side).
Factor completely, then set EACH factor equal to zero and solve — this is the Zero Product Property.
A quadratic can have 0, 1, or 2 real solutions.

concepts.intro: Works for ANY quadratic equation, even ones that don't factor nicely.
b: For ax² + bx + c = 0: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.
Identify a, b, and c carefully from the standard form BEFORE plugging in — a common source of errors.
The ± means you'll generally get two answers: one using + and one using −.

concepts.intro: Every quadratic function graphs as a U-shaped curve called a parabola.
b: If a > 0, the parabola opens UP (has a minimum). If a < 0, it opens DOWN (has a maximum).
Axis of symmetry: x = −b/2a — a vertical line through the vertex that splits the parabola into two mirror halves.
The vertex is the highest or lowest point; find its y-coordinate by plugging the axis-of-symmetry x-value back into the function.

concepts.intro: The expression under the square root in the quadratic formula tells you how many real solutions exist, without solving.
b: Discriminant = b² − 4ac.
If b² − 4ac > 0: two different real solutions (the parabola crosses the x-axis twice).
If b² − 4ac = 0: exactly one real solution (the parabola just touches the x-axis at its vertex).
If b² − 4ac < 0: no real solutions (the parabola never touches the x-axis).

traps: Forgetting to set the quadratic equal to ZERO before factoring — the Zero Product Property only works when one side is 0.
Sign errors plugging into the quadratic formula, especially when b or c is already negative — use parentheses around each substituted value.
Confusing the discriminant's sign meaning: POSITIVE discriminant means TWO solutions, not one.
fms: Zero Product Property: if AB = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a
Axis of symmetry: x = −b/2a · Discriminant: b² − 4ac

units.name: Radicals & Rational Exponents

concepts.intro: Simplify a radical by pulling out the largest perfect-square factor.
b: Find the largest perfect square that divides evenly into the number under the radical.
A radical is fully simplified when no perfect-square factor remains inside it.

concepts.intro: Radicals combine like variables — you can only add/subtract 'like radicals.'
b: Like radicals have the SAME number under the root: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2 (add the coefficients, keep the radical).
√2 + √3 CANNOT be combined — they are not like radicals.
Multiplying radicals: √a · √b = √(ab). Multiply what's under the roots together, then simplify.

concepts.intro: Rational (fraction) exponents are just another way to write roots.
b: x^(m/n) = ⁿ√(x^m) = (ⁿ√x)^m — the denominator is the root, the numerator is the power.
All the normal exponent laws (product, quotient, power rules) still apply to rational exponents.

concepts.intro: To undo a square root, square both sides — but this can introduce a fake answer you must check for.
b: Isolate the radical on one side first, then square both sides to eliminate it.
Solve the resulting equation normally.
ALWAYS check your answer(s) in the ORIGINAL equation — squaring can create an 'extraneous' (fake) solution that doesn't actually work.

traps: √2 + √3 does NOT equal √5 — you cannot add unlike radicals by adding what's under the root.
Forgetting to check for extraneous solutions after squaring both sides of a radical equation — this is tested constantly.
x^(m/n): the DENOMINATOR n is the root, the NUMERATOR m is the power — easy to flip by accident.
fms: √(ab) = √a · √b · Combine only LIKE radicals
Radical equations: isolate radical, square both sides, CHECK for extraneous solutions

units.name: Exponential Functions & Sequences

concepts.intro: Exponential functions model quantities that grow or shrink by a constant PERCENT each time period, not a constant amount.
b: General form: y = a(1 + r)ᵗ for growth, y = a(1 − r)ᵗ for decay, where a is the starting amount and r is the rate (as a decimal).
The base (1 + r) or (1 − r) is called the growth/decay factor — if it's greater than 1, it's growth; if it's between 0 and 1, it's decay.
Unlike linear growth (constant amount added each time), exponential growth compounds — it multiplies by the same factor each period.

concepts.intro: A sequence where you ADD the same number (the common difference) to get the next term.
b: Common difference d = any term minus the term before it.
Explicit formula: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d, where a₁ is the first term.
Arithmetic sequences correspond to LINEAR functions — the graph of term number vs. value is a straight line.

concepts.intro: A sequence where you MULTIPLY by the same number (the common ratio) to get the next term.
b: Common ratio r = any term divided by the term before it.
Explicit formula: aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1), where a₁ is the first term.
Geometric sequences correspond to EXPONENTIAL functions.

concepts.intro: Knowing which model fits a situation is a core skill to know.
b: Linear/arithmetic: same amount ADDED each period (+3 every year).
Exponential/geometric: same PERCENT or FACTOR multiplied each period (×1.05 every year, or ×2 every hour).
Over a long enough time, exponential growth will always eventually overtake linear growth, no matter the starting values.

traps: Mixing up common difference (arithmetic, addition) with common ratio (geometric, multiplication) — check whether you're adding or multiplying between terms.
In y = a(1+r)ᵗ, r is written as a DECIMAL (5% is 0.05, not 5), and you add/subtract it from 1 before raising to the t power.
aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d uses (n − 1), not n — a common off-by-one error.
fms: Exponential: y = a(1 ± r)ᵗ
Arithmetic: aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d (common difference d)
Geometric: aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1) (common ratio r)

units.name: Statistics: Data & Distributions

concepts.intro: Mean, median, and mode each describe the 'typical' value of a data set differently.
b: Mean: sum of all values divided by the count. Sensitive to outliers (extreme values pull it strongly).
Median: the middle value when data is ordered (average the two middle values if there's an even count). Resistant to outliers.
Mode: the most frequently occurring value(s). A data set can have no mode, one mode, or multiple modes.

concepts.intro: Spread describes how varied or consistent the data is.
b: Range = maximum − minimum. The simplest measure of spread, but very sensitive to outliers.
Interquartile Range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1 (the range of the middle 50% of the data) — resistant to outliers.
Standard deviation measures the typical distance each data point is from the mean; a bigger standard deviation means more spread-out data.

concepts.intro: A box plot visually displays five key statistics at once.
b: The five numbers, in order: minimum, Q1 (first quartile), median (Q2), Q3 (third quartile), maximum.
The 'box' spans from Q1 to Q3 (the IQR); the line inside the box is the median; the 'whiskers' extend to the min and max.
An outlier is often flagged if it falls more than 1.5 × IQR beyond Q1 or Q3.

concepts.intro: The overall shape of a histogram tells you a lot about the data before you compute a single statistic.
b: Symmetric (roughly bell-shaped/normal): mean ≈ median.
Skewed right (tail stretches toward higher values): mean is pulled HIGHER than the median.
Skewed left (tail stretches toward lower values): mean is pulled LOWER than the median.

traps: Mean is pulled toward the tail in a skewed distribution — 'skewed right' means the mean is greater than the median, which feels backwards to many students.
Forgetting to order the data before finding the median — an unordered 'middle value' is meaningless.
IQR uses Q3 − Q1, NOT max − min (that's the range).
fms: Mean = sum ÷ count · Median = middle value (ordered data)
Range = max − min · IQR = Q3 − Q1
Skewed right: mean > median · Skewed left: mean < median

units.name: Statistics: Regression & Correlation

concepts.intro: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numerical variables.
b: Positive association: as x increases, y tends to increase (points trend upward left to right).
Negative association: as x increases, y tends to decrease (points trend downward left to right).
No association: no clear pattern — the points look scattered randomly.

concepts.intro: A line of best fit summarizes the overall trend in a scatter plot with linear association.
b: The line of best fit (regression line) minimizes the overall distance between itself and all the data points.
Its equation has the same form as any line, ŷ = mx + b, and can be used to PREDICT y-values for given x-values.
Predicting within the range of the given data is called interpolation (generally reliable); predicting far outside the given range is extrapolation (much less reliable).

concepts.intro: r is a single number from −1 to 1 that measures how strong and what direction a LINEAR relationship is.
b: r close to +1: strong positive linear correlation. r close to −1: strong negative linear correlation.
r close to 0: little to no linear correlation (the data may still have a pattern, just not a linear one).
The closer |r| is to 1, the more tightly the points cluster around the regression line.

concepts.intro: A strong correlation does NOT prove that one variable causes the other to change.
b: Two variables can be strongly correlated because of a third, unseen variable — or by pure coincidence.
Only a controlled experiment (not just observed data) can establish causation.
A residual is the difference between an actual data point and the value the regression line predicts for it — residuals scattered randomly around 0 suggest a linear model is a good fit.

traps: A strong correlation (r near ±1) does NOT mean one variable CAUSES the other — this is tested directly and often.
r = 0 doesn't mean 'no relationship at all' — it means no LINEAR relationship; the data could still follow a strong curved pattern.
Extrapolating far beyond the collected data range is unreliable, even with a strong r value.
fms: −1 ≤ r ≤ 1 · closer to ±1 = stronger linear correlation
Positive association: y increases with x · Negative: y decreases as x increases
Correlation ≠ Causation

units.name: Functions: Notation, Domain/Range & Transformations

concepts.intro: f(x) is just a labeled way of writing 'y' that tells you exactly which function produced the value.
b: f(x) is read 'f of x' — it means the OUTPUT of function f when the input is x. It does NOT mean f times x.
To evaluate f(3), substitute 3 everywhere you see x in the function's rule.

concepts.intro: Domain is every valid input; range is every possible output.
b: Domain: the set of all possible x-values (inputs) a function can accept.
Range: the set of all possible y-values (outputs) a function can produce.
Common domain restrictions: you cannot divide by zero, and you cannot take the square root of a negative number (in the real numbers).

concepts.intro: A relation is a function only if every input maps to exactly ONE output.
b: Vertical Line Test: if any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, it is NOT a function.
In a table or set of ordered pairs, a function cannot repeat an x-value with two different y-values.
A relation CAN repeat a y-value for different x-values and still be a function — only repeated x-values (with different outputs) break it.

concepts.intro: Simple changes to a function's equation shift, flip, or stretch its graph in predictable ways.
b: f(x) + k shifts the graph UP k units (k > 0) or down (k < 0). f(x + k) shifts LEFT k units (k > 0) or right (k < 0) — horizontal shifts feel backwards.
−f(x) reflects the graph over the x-axis; f(−x) reflects it over the y-axis.
Average rate of change between two points = (change in y) ÷ (change in x) — for a linear function this is just the slope; for other functions it changes depending on which interval you pick.

traps: f(x) does NOT mean f multiplied by x — it means the output of function f for input x.
Horizontal shifts feel backwards: f(x − 3) shifts RIGHT, not left. Vertical shifts feel normal: f(x) − 3 shifts DOWN.
A relation with a repeated y-value is still fine — only a repeated x-value with two different outputs makes it NOT a function.
fms: f(x) = output of function f at input x
Vertical Line Test: crosses more than once → not a function
Avg. rate of change = (change in y) / (change in x)

flashcards.d: Operations that undo each other: addition/subtraction, multiplication/division. Used to isolate a variable.
An equation with more than one variable, solved for one variable in terms of the others.
Two inequalities joined together, like −3 < x ≤ 5, describing a range of values.
When solving leads to a false statement (like 5 = 8) — no value of the variable works.
When solving leads to a true statement (like 5 = 5) — every value of the variable works.
Absolute value equation meaning x = a or x = −a (for a > 0).
Steepness of a line: m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), or 'rise over run.'
y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), used to write an equation from one point and a slope.
The slope of a vertical line (x = constant) — division by zero, so it has no numeric value.
The slope of a horizontal line (y = constant).
Negative reciprocals of each other (multiply to −1). Example: 2 and −½.
The point where a line crosses the x-axis; found by setting y = 0.
Two or more equations considered together; the solution is the point (x, y) that satisfies all of them.
Solving a system by solving one equation for a variable and plugging that expression into the other equation.
Solving a system by adding or subtracting the equations to cancel out one variable.
When two lines are parallel (same slope, different intercept) — they never intersect.
When two equations describe the exact same line (same slope AND intercept).
xᵃ · xᵇ = x^(a+b) — multiplying same bases adds the exponents.
(xᵃ)ᵇ = x^(ab) — a power raised to a power multiplies the exponents.
Any nonzero base raised to the 0 power equals 1: x⁰ = 1.
x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ — flips the base to the denominator and makes the exponent positive.
Polynomials with one, two, and three terms, respectively.
The highest exponent on the variable in the polynomial.
First, Outer, Inner, Last — the order for multiplying two binomials together.
The largest number/variable expression that divides evenly into every term — factor this out first.
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). There is no similar pattern for a sum of squares.
Splitting a polynomial into pairs of terms, factoring each pair's GCF, then factoring out the shared binomial.
Keep factoring until no factor can be broken down any further (always check for a GCF first).
If A · B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0. The basis for solving factored quadratics.
x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, used to solve any quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0.
The highest or lowest point of a parabola; occurs on the axis of symmetry.
The vertical line x = −b/2a that splits a parabola into two mirror-image halves.
b² − 4ac. Positive → 2 real solutions; zero → 1 real solution; negative → 0 real solutions.
Pulling the largest perfect-square factor out from under the root sign.
Radicals with the same number under the root — only like radicals can be added or subtracted.
x^(m/n) = ⁿ√(xᵐ) — the denominator is the root, the numerator is the power.
A solution produced by squaring both sides of a radical equation that does not actually work in the original equation.
y = a(1 + r)ᵗ — a quantity that grows by the same PERCENT each time period.
y = a(1 − r)ᵗ — a quantity that shrinks by the same PERCENT each time period.
A sequence where the same number (common difference) is added to get each next term.
The constant amount added between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.
A sequence where each term is multiplied by the same number (common ratio) to get the next term.
The constant factor multiplied between consecutive terms of a geometric sequence.
The sum of all data values divided by the number of values; sensitive to outliers.
The middle value of ordered data; resistant to outliers.
The most frequently occurring value(s) in a data set.
Maximum value minus minimum value.
Q3 − Q1; the range of the middle 50% of the data, resistant to outliers.
A distribution with a tail stretching toward higher values; mean is greater than median.
A distribution with a tail stretching toward lower values; mean is less than median.
As one variable increases, the other tends to increase too (upward trend on a scatter plot).
As one variable increases, the other tends to decrease (downward trend on a scatter plot).
A line that summarizes the trend in a scatter plot and can be used to make predictions.
A number from −1 to 1 measuring the strength and direction of a LINEAR relationship.
The difference between an actual data value and the value predicted by the regression line.
A strong correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other.
Read 'f of x' — the output of function f when the input is x. Not f multiplied by x.
The set of all valid input (x) values for a function.
The set of all possible output (y) values a function can produce.
If any vertical line crosses a graph more than once, the graph does NOT represent a function.
(change in y) ÷ (change in x) between two points on a function.

quiz.q: Solve for x: 3x + 5 = 20
Solve for x: 2(x − 4) = 10
Solve for x: 5x − 3 = 2x + 12
Solve the literal equation A = ½bh for h
quiz.e: Multiply both sides by 2, then divide by b: h = 2A/b.

quiz.q: Solve the literal equation I = Prt for r
quiz.e: Divide both sides by Pt: r = I/(Pt).

quiz.q: Solve the inequality: −2x + 6 > 10
quiz.e: −2x > 4 → x < −2 (flip the sign when dividing by a negative).

quiz.q: Solve the inequality: 4x − 7 ≤ 9
Which equation has infinite solutions?
quiz.e: 2x + 3 = 2x + 3 simplifies to a true statement (3 = 3) for every x, so it has infinite solutions.

quiz.q: Which equation has no solution?
quiz.e: 3x + 1 = 3x + 4 simplifies to 1 = 4, a false statement — no value of x works.

quiz.q: Solve |x − 2| = 7
Which interval represents |x| < 4?
quiz.e: |x| < a means −a < x < a, so −4 < x < 4.

quiz.q: Which interval represents |x| > 3?
quiz.e: |x| > a means x < −a or x > a.

quiz.q: Solve for x: −3(x + 2) = 15
Find the slope between (2, 3) and (6, 11)
Find the slope between (−1, 5) and (3, −3)
What is the slope of the line y = −3x + 7?
quiz.e: In y = mx + b form, m = −3.

quiz.q: What is the y-intercept of y = 5x − 2?
quiz.e: In y = mx + b form, b = −2.

quiz.q: A line has y-intercept 4 and slope −2. What is its equation?
quiz.e: y = mx + b with m = −2, b = 4.

quiz.q: Find the equation (in y = mx + b form) of the line with slope 3 through the point (2, 1)
A line is parallel to y = 4x − 1. What is its slope?
quiz.e: Parallel lines have the same slope.

quiz.q: A line is perpendicular to y = 2x + 3. What is its slope?
quiz.e: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: the negative reciprocal of 2 is −1/2.

quiz.q: Which of these lines is horizontal?
quiz.e: y = 5 is a constant y-value for every x — a horizontal line.

quiz.q: What is the slope of a vertical line?
quiz.e: A vertical line's slope is undefined (division by zero in the slope formula).

quiz.q: Find the x-intercept of 2x + 3y = 12
Find the y-intercept of 2x + 3y = 12
Two lines have slopes 2/3 and −3/2. What is their relationship?
quiz.e: (2/3)(−3/2) = −1, so the lines are perpendicular.

quiz.q: Solve by substitution: y = x + 2 and 2x + y = 11
Solve by elimination: x + y = 10 and x − y = 2
quiz.e: Adding the equations: 2x = 12 → x = 6, then y = 4.

quiz.q: Solve by substitution: y = 2x and x + y = 9
Solve: 2x + 3y = 12 and 2x − y = 4
quiz.e: Subtracting: (2x+3y)−(2x−y) = 12−4 → 4y = 8 → y = 2. Then 2x − 2 = 4 → x = 3.

quiz.q: How many solutions does the system y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x − 4 have?
quiz.e: Same slope (3), different y-intercepts — the lines are parallel and never meet.

quiz.q: How many solutions does the system y = 2x + 5 and 2y = 4x + 10 have?
quiz.e: Dividing the second equation by 2 gives y = 2x + 5 — the exact same line, so infinite solutions.

quiz.q: How many solutions does the system x + y = 7 and x − y = 1 have?
quiz.e: The lines have different slopes (−1 and 1), so they cross exactly once.

quiz.q: A system has two equations with the same slope but different y-intercepts. What do the graphs look like?
quiz.e: Same slope, different intercept — always parallel, never intersecting.

quiz.q: Solve: x + 2y = 8 and 3x − 2y = 8
quiz.e: Adding the equations: 4x = 16 → x = 4. Then 4 + 2y = 8 → y = 2.

quiz.q: When graphing y > 2x − 1, how should the boundary line be drawn?
quiz.e: Strict inequality (>) means a dashed line; shade above since y is greater than the line.

quiz.q: How do you determine which side of a boundary line to shade?
o: Test a point not on the line in the original inequality
quiz.e: Plug a test point (often the origin) into the original inequality — if true, shade that side.

quiz.q: The solution region for a system of two linear inequalities is:
o: The union of both shaded regions
The region where both shaded areas overlap
quiz.e: A system's solution must satisfy BOTH inequalities — only the overlap works.

quiz.q: Solve: 4x − y = 9 and x + y = 6
quiz.e: Adding the equations: 5x = 15 → x = 3. Then 3 + y = 6 → y = 3.

quiz.q: Simplify: x⁴ · x³
quiz.e: Product rule: add the exponents, 4 + 3 = 7.

quiz.q: Simplify: x⁹ / x⁴
quiz.e: Quotient rule: subtract the exponents, 9 − 4 = 5.

quiz.q: Simplify: (x³)⁴
quiz.e: Power rule: multiply the exponents, 3 × 4 = 12.

quiz.q: Simplify: x⁰ (x ≠ 0)
quiz.e: Any nonzero number raised to the 0 power equals 1.

quiz.q: Simplify: x⁻³
quiz.e: A negative exponent flips the base to the denominator: x⁻³ = 1/x³.

quiz.q: Simplify: (2x²)³
quiz.e: Cube both factors: 2³ = 8 and (x²)³ = x⁶, giving 8x⁶.

quiz.q: What is the degree of 5x³ − 2x + 7?
quiz.e: The degree is the highest exponent present, which is 3.

quiz.q: Classify x² + 3x − 1 by its number of terms
quiz.e: It has three terms: x², 3x, and −1.
Combine like terms: (3x²+x²)=4x², (2x−4x)=−2x, (−5+1)=−4.

quiz.q: Subtract: (5x² + 3x) − (2x² − x)
quiz.e: Distribute the negative: 5x²+3x−2x²+x = 3x²+4x.

quiz.q: Multiply: (x + 3)(x + 5)
quiz.e: FOIL: x² + 5x + 3x + 15 = x² + 8x + 15.

quiz.q: Multiply: (x − 4)(x + 4)
quiz.e: This is a difference-of-squares pattern: x² − 16.

quiz.q: Multiply: 3x(2x² − 5x + 1)
quiz.e: Distribute 3x to every term: 6x³ − 15x² + 3x.

quiz.q: Factor completely: 6x² + 9x
quiz.e: The GCF of 6x² and 9x is 3x: 3x(2x + 3).

quiz.q: Factor: x² + 7x + 12
quiz.e: Need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7: 3 and 4.

quiz.q: Factor: x² − 2x − 15
quiz.e: Need two numbers that multiply to −15 and add to −2: −5 and 3.

quiz.q: Factor: x² − 9x + 20
quiz.e: Need two numbers that multiply to 20 and add to −9: −4 and −5.

quiz.q: Factor: x² − 16
quiz.e: Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b), with a=x, b=4.

quiz.q: Factor: 4x² − 25
quiz.e: Difference of squares: (2x)² − 5² = (2x−5)(2x+5).

quiz.q: Factor: x² + 10x + 25
quiz.e: This is a perfect square trinomial: (x+5)(x+5) = (x+5)².

quiz.q: Which expression does NOT factor over the real numbers?
quiz.e: A sum of squares like x² + 9 has no real-number factoring pattern.

quiz.q: Factor completely: 2x² + 8x + 8
quiz.e: Pull out the GCF of 2 first: 2(x² + 4x + 4) = 2(x+2)².

quiz.q: Factor by grouping: x³ + 3x² + 2x + 6
What should you always check for first when factoring any polynomial?
quiz.e: Always pull out a GCF first — it makes every later step simpler.

quiz.q: Factor: x² − x − 6
quiz.e: Need two numbers that multiply to −6 and add to −1: −3 and 2.

quiz.q: Factor completely: 3x² + 9x − 12
quiz.e: Pull out the GCF of 3: 3(x² + 3x − 4) = 3(x+4)(x−1).

quiz.q: Solve by factoring: x² − 5x + 6 = 0
Solve: x² − 9 = 0
Solve: x² + 4x = 0
Use the quadratic formula to solve x² + 2x − 8 = 0
Use the quadratic formula to solve x² − 4x + 4 = 0
quiz.e: Discriminant = 16−16=0, so there's exactly one solution: x=(4±0)/2=2.

quiz.q: For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant is:
quiz.e: The discriminant is the expression under the square root: b² − 4ac.

quiz.q: A quadratic has discriminant = −12. How many real solutions does it have?
quiz.e: A negative discriminant means no real solutions (the parabola never touches the x-axis).

quiz.q: A quadratic has discriminant = 25. How many real solutions does it have?
quiz.e: A positive discriminant means two distinct real solutions.

quiz.q: A quadratic has discriminant = 0. How many real solutions does it have?
quiz.e: A discriminant of exactly 0 means one real solution (the vertex touches the x-axis).

quiz.q: For y = 2x² − 8x + 3, does the parabola open up or down?
quiz.e: Since a = 2 > 0, the parabola opens upward.

quiz.q: Find the axis of symmetry for y = x² − 6x + 5
quiz.e: Axis of symmetry: x = −b/2a = −(−6)/2(1) = 3.

quiz.q: Find the axis of symmetry for y = 2x² + 8x + 1
quiz.e: Axis of symmetry: x = −b/2a = −8/(2·2) = −2.

quiz.q: The vertex of a parabola is:
o: Where it crosses the x-axis twice
The highest or lowest point on the curve
quiz.e: The vertex is the maximum point (if it opens down) or minimum point (if it opens up).

quiz.q: Solve: x² = 49
quiz.e: Taking the square root of both sides gives x = ±7.

quiz.q: Simplify √48
Simplify √72
Simplify √20
Simplify: 3√2 + 5√2
quiz.e: Like radicals combine by adding coefficients: (3+5)√2 = 8√2.

quiz.q: Simplify: 7√3 − 2√3
quiz.e: Like radicals: (7−2)√3 = 5√3.

quiz.q: Which expression CANNOT be simplified by combining like radicals?
quiz.e: √2 and √3 have different numbers under the root — they are not like radicals.

quiz.q: Multiply: √3 · √12
Which expression equals x^(1/2)?
quiz.e: A power of 1/n equals the nth root: x^(1/2) = √x.

quiz.q: Which expression equals x^(2/3)?
Solve: √(x + 3) = 5
quiz.e: Square both sides: x+3=25 → x=22. Check: √25=5 ✓.

quiz.q: Solve: √(2x − 1) = 3
quiz.e: Square both sides: 2x−1=9 → x=5. Check: √9=3 ✓.

quiz.q: Solve: √x = −4
quiz.e: Squaring gives x=16, but √16=4, not −4 — this is extraneous, so there is no real solution.

quiz.q: Why must you check solutions to radical equations in the original equation?
o: Squaring both sides can introduce extraneous solutions
It isn't necessary if you show work
quiz.e: Squaring both sides can create solutions that don't actually satisfy the original equation.

quiz.q: A population of 500 grows 6% per year. Which equation models this?
quiz.e: Growth: y = a(1+r)ᵗ with a=500, r=0.06.

quiz.q: A car worth $20,000 depreciates 10% per year. Which equation models its value?
quiz.e: Decay: y = a(1−r)ᵗ with a=20000, r=0.10, so the factor is 0.9.

quiz.q: In y = a(1 + r)ᵗ, if r = 0.08, this represents:
quiz.e: r as a decimal of 0.08 means an 8% growth rate.

quiz.q: In y = a(1 − r)ᵗ, if r = 0.15, this represents:
quiz.e: Subtracting r means decay — a 15% decay rate.

quiz.q: Find the common difference: 4, 9, 14, 19, ...
quiz.e: Each term increases by 5 (9−4=5, 14−9=5).

quiz.q: Find the common ratio: 3, 6, 12, 24, ...
quiz.e: Each term is multiplied by 2 (6/3=2, 12/6=2).

quiz.q: Find the 10th term of the arithmetic sequence with a₁ = 3, d = 4
Find the 6th term of the geometric sequence with a₁ = 2, r = 3
Find the 5th term of the arithmetic sequence 7, 11, 15, 19, ...
Is the sequence 2, 4, 8, 16, ... arithmetic or geometric?
quiz.e: Each term is multiplied by 2 (a constant ratio), so it's geometric.

quiz.q: Is the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, ... arithmetic or geometric?
quiz.e: Each term increases by 3 (a constant difference), so it's arithmetic.

quiz.q: Which grows faster in the long run: linear growth or exponential growth?
o: They grow at the same rate
It depends only on the y-intercept
quiz.e: No matter the starting values, exponential growth eventually outpaces linear growth.

quiz.q: The explicit formula for an arithmetic sequence is:
quiz.e: Arithmetic sequences add the common difference d, using (n−1) steps from the first term.

quiz.q: Find the mean of 4, 7, 9, 12, 13
quiz.e: Sum = 45, divided by 5 values = 9.

quiz.q: Find the median of 3, 8, 5, 12, 9
quiz.e: Ordered: 3, 5, 8, 9, 12 — the middle value is 8.

quiz.q: Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 8
quiz.e: With an even count, average the two middle values: (4+6)/2 = 5.

quiz.q: Find the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 8
quiz.e: 3 appears three times, more than any other value.

quiz.q: Find the range of 12, 5, 19, 8, 3
quiz.e: Range = max − min = 19 − 3 = 16.

quiz.q: A data set has Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 22. Find the IQR.
Which measure of center is LEAST affected by an outlier?
quiz.e: The median only depends on the middle position, not the actual size of extreme values.

quiz.q: In a box plot, the line inside the box represents the:
quiz.e: The line inside the box marks the median (Q2).

quiz.q: In a box plot, the box itself spans from:
quiz.e: The box represents the interquartile range, from Q1 to Q3.

quiz.q: A distribution is skewed right. Which is true?
quiz.e: A right-skewed tail pulls the mean higher than the median.

quiz.q: A distribution is skewed left. Which is true?
quiz.e: A left-skewed tail pulls the mean lower than the median.

quiz.q: Which measure of spread is MOST resistant to outliers?
quiz.e: IQR only uses the middle 50% of data, so extreme outliers don't affect it.

quiz.q: For the data set 1, 2, 3, 4, 100 — which measure of center is most affected by the outlier 100?
quiz.e: The mean is pulled dramatically higher by the outlier; the median stays at 3.

quiz.q: A scatter plot shows points trending upward from left to right. This shows:
quiz.e: An upward trend means as x increases, y tends to increase — positive association.

quiz.q: A scatter plot shows points trending downward from left to right. This shows:
quiz.e: A downward trend means as x increases, y tends to decrease — negative association.

quiz.q: A correlation coefficient of r = 0.95 indicates:
quiz.e: r close to +1 means a strong positive linear correlation.

quiz.q: A correlation coefficient of r = −0.88 indicates:
quiz.e: r close to −1 means a strong negative linear correlation.

quiz.q: A correlation coefficient close to r = 0.05 indicates:
quiz.e: r near 0 means little to no LINEAR relationship.

quiz.q: Which value of r shows the STRONGEST linear relationship?
quiz.e: Strength depends on |r| — |−0.91| = 0.91 is closest to 1.

quiz.q: The line that minimizes overall distance to all points on a scatter plot is called the:
quiz.e: This is the regression line, or line of best fit.

quiz.q: A residual is:
o: The slope of the regression line
The difference between an actual value and the predicted value
quiz.e: A residual = actual y − predicted y for a given data point.

quiz.q: Predicting a y-value using an x-value far outside the range of the collected data is called:
quiz.e: Extrapolation goes beyond the collected data range and is less reliable.

quiz.q: A strong correlation between ice cream sales and drowning incidents does NOT mean ice cream causes drowning because:
o: A third variable (like hot weather) likely explains both
The correlation coefficient must be negative
Causation only applies to negative correlations
quiz.e: A lurking (third) variable — like summer heat — likely drives both.

quiz.q: If r = 1 exactly, the data points:
o: Lie exactly on a line with positive slope
Lie exactly on a line with negative slope
Form a curve, not a line
quiz.e: r = 1 is a perfect positive linear correlation — every point lies exactly on the line.

quiz.q: Interpolation means predicting a value:
o: Within the range of the collected data
Far outside the range of the collected data
quiz.e: Interpolation stays within the range of the data already collected, so it's more reliable.

quiz.q: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f(4)
If f(x) = x² − 1, find f(3)
If f(x) = 3x − 5, find f(−2)
If g(x) = x² + 2x, find g(−1)
What does f(x) mean?
o: The output of function f for input x
quiz.e: f(x) is notation for 'the output of f when the input is x' — not multiplication.

quiz.q: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 3)?
quiz.e: The denominator cannot equal 0, so x ≠ 3.

quiz.q: What is the domain of f(x) = √(x − 5)?
quiz.e: The expression under the root cannot be negative: x − 5 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 5.

quiz.q: Which test determines if a graph represents a function?
quiz.e: The Vertical Line Test: if any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, it's not a function.

quiz.q: A relation contains the points (2, 3), (2, 5), (4, 7). Is this a function?
o: No, x = 2 has two different outputs
quiz.e: x = 2 maps to both 3 and 5 — a function cannot have one input with two different outputs.

quiz.q: A relation contains the points (1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 6). Is this a function?
o: Yes, every x has exactly one output
No, y = 4 repeats so it's not a function
Yes, but only if x-values are consecutive
quiz.e: Repeated y-values are fine — a function is only broken by a repeated x-value with different outputs.

quiz.q: The graph of f(x) + 3 compared to f(x) is shifted:
quiz.e: Adding outside the function shifts the graph vertically — up 3 units.

quiz.q: The graph of f(x − 2) compared to f(x) is shifted:
quiz.e: Subtracting inside the function shifts the graph right — horizontal shifts feel backwards.

quiz.q: Find the average rate of change of f(x) = x² between x = 1 and x = 3
quiz.e: f(1)=1, f(3)=9. Average rate of change = (9−1)/(3−1) = 8/2 = 4.

quiz.q: Solve for x: 6x − 4 = 2x + 12
Solve for x: −5x + 3 = 18
Solve the literal equation for w: P = 2l + 2w
Solve the inequality: 5 − 2x ≤ 11
quiz.e: −2x ≤ 6 → x ≥ −3 (flip the sign when dividing by a negative).

quiz.q: Which value of x satisfies |2x − 4| = 10?
Graph the solution to x > 5 on a number line. What kind of circle is used at 5?
quiz.e: Strict inequality (>) uses an open circle, since 5 itself is not included.

quiz.q: Find the slope between (0, 0) and (4, −8)
What is the y-intercept of y = −4x + 9?
quiz.e: In y=mx+b form, b=9.

quiz.q: Write the equation of the line through (0, −3) with slope 5
quiz.e: y = mx+b with m=5, b=−3.

quiz.q: A line is parallel to x = 7. Which of these could be its equation?
quiz.e: Vertical lines (x=constant) are parallel to other vertical lines.

quiz.q: Find the x-intercept of y = 3x − 12
Two lines have slopes −4 and 1/4. What is their relationship?
quiz.e: (−4)(1/4) = −1, so they are perpendicular.

quiz.q: Write the equation, in slope-intercept form, of the line through (4, 5) and (4, −1)
quiz.e: Both points share x=4, making this a vertical line — it has no slope-intercept form.

quiz.q: Solve by substitution: x = 3y and 2x + y = 21
Solve by elimination: 2x + y = 9 and x − y = 3
quiz.e: Adding: 3x=12 → x=4, then y=9−8=1.

quiz.q: How many solutions does x − y = 4 and 2x − 2y = 8 have?
quiz.e: Dividing the second equation by 2 gives x−y=4, the same line — infinite solutions.

quiz.q: Solve: 4x − 3y = 1 and 2x + 3y = 11
quiz.e: Adding: 6x=12 → x=2. Then 8−3y=1 → y=7/3.

quiz.q: A system has one solution. What must be true about the two lines' slopes?
quiz.e: Different slopes guarantee the lines cross at exactly one point.

quiz.q: Graphing y ≤ −x + 2, which type of boundary line and shading is used?
quiz.e: ≤ uses a solid line (included); shade below since y is less than or equal to the line.

quiz.q: Solve: y = 4 − x and x + y = 4
quiz.e: Substituting: x + (4−x) = 4 → 4=4, always true — the equations describe the same line.

quiz.q: Simplify: (3x)² · x
quiz.e: (3x)²=9x², then times x gives 9x³.

quiz.q: Simplify: x¹² / x³
quiz.e: Subtract exponents: 12−3=9.

quiz.q: Simplify: (x⁻²)³
quiz.e: Multiply exponents: −2×3=−6.

quiz.q: What is the degree of the polynomial 7x⁴y² + 3xy?
quiz.e: Degree of a term is the sum of its exponents; 7x⁴y² has degree 4+2=6, the highest in the polynomial.

quiz.q: Multiply: (2x − 1)(x + 5)
quiz.e: FOIL: 2x²+10x−x−5 = 2x²+9x−5.

quiz.q: Simplify: (x²)⁰
quiz.e: Anything nonzero to the 0 power is 1.

quiz.q: Factor: x² − 25
quiz.e: Difference of squares: x² − 5² = (x−5)(x+5).

quiz.q: Factor: x² + 12x + 36
quiz.e: Perfect square trinomial: (x+6)(x+6) = (x+6)².

quiz.q: Factor: x² + x − 20
quiz.e: Need two numbers that multiply to −20 and add to 1: 5 and −4.

quiz.q: Factor completely: 5x² − 20
quiz.e: GCF of 5 first: 5(x²−4) = 5(x−2)(x+2).

quiz.q: Factor: x² − 3x − 18
quiz.e: Need two numbers that multiply to −18 and add to −3: −6 and 3.

quiz.q: Which of these is a difference of squares?
quiz.e: x² − 49 = x² − 7² fits the a²−b² pattern.

quiz.q: Factor by grouping: x³ + 5x² + 2x + 10
Solve by factoring: x² + x − 12 = 0
Solve: x² − 25 = 0
Use the quadratic formula to solve x² − 6x + 5 = 0
A quadratic has discriminant = 0. Describe its graph.
o: It touches the x-axis at exactly one point (the vertex)
quiz.e: A zero discriminant means one repeated real solution — the vertex sits exactly on the x-axis.

quiz.q: For y = −3x² + 12x − 5, does the parabola open up or down?
quiz.e: Since a=−3 < 0, the parabola opens downward.

quiz.q: Find the axis of symmetry for y = x² + 4x − 1
Solve: 2x² = 32
Simplify √75
Simplify √32
Simplify: 4√5 + 3√5
quiz.e: Like radicals: (4+3)√5 = 7√5.

quiz.q: Simplify: √6 · √3
Simplify x^(3/2) using radical notation
quiz.e: x^(3/2) = √(x³) (the denominator 2 is the root, numerator 3 is the power).

quiz.q: Solve √(3x) = 9
quiz.e: Square both sides: 3x=81 → x=27.

quiz.q: Solve √(x − 1) = −3
quiz.e: Squaring gives x=10, but √9=3≠−3 — extraneous, so there's no real solution.

quiz.q: A population of 800 declines 4% per year. Which equation models this?
quiz.e: Decay factor is 1−0.04=0.96.

quiz.q: Find the common difference: 20, 15, 10, 5, ...
quiz.e: Each term decreases by 5.

quiz.q: Find the common ratio: 1, 1/3, 1/9, 1/27, ...
quiz.e: Each term is multiplied by 1/3.

quiz.q: Find the 12th term of the arithmetic sequence with a₁ = 6, d = 2
Find the 4th term of the geometric sequence with a₁ = 5, r = 4
Which type of sequence corresponds to a LINEAR function?
quiz.e: Arithmetic sequences (constant difference) match linear functions.

quiz.q: In y = a(1+r)ᵗ, what does 'a' represent?
quiz.e: 'a' is the starting amount before any growth or decay is applied.

quiz.q: Find the mean of 6, 10, 14, 18, 22
quiz.e: Sum=70, divided by 5 = 14.

quiz.q: Find the median of 9, 2, 7, 4, 11, 6
quiz.e: Ordered: 2,4,6,7,9,11 — average the two middle values (6,7): 6.5.

quiz.q: Find the range of 45, 12, 38, 7, 29
quiz.e: Range = max − min = 45 − 7 = 38.

quiz.q: A data set has Q1=15 and Q3=27. Find the IQR
In a box plot, what does a longer whisker on one side suggest?
o: More spread out data on that side
quiz.e: A longer whisker indicates the data extends further and is more spread out on that side.

quiz.q: Which measure of center would be most useful for a strongly skewed data set?
quiz.e: The median resists the pull of extreme values, making it more representative in a skewed distribution.

quiz.q: A histogram has a long tail extending to the left. How does this describe the distribution?
quiz.e: A distribution is named for the direction its tail stretches — a left-stretching tail means skewed left.

quiz.q: A scatter plot shows no clear pattern between x and y. What kind of association is this?
quiz.e: Randomly scattered points with no trend indicate no association.

quiz.q: Which correlation coefficient indicates the weakest linear relationship?
quiz.e: |0.02| is closest to 0, indicating almost no linear relationship.

quiz.q: A line of best fit is ŷ = −2x + 50. What does the slope tell you?
o: y decreases by 2 for every 1 unit increase in x
y increases by 2 for every 1 unit increase in x
x decreases by 2 for every unit of y
quiz.e: The slope −2 means y decreases by 2 units for each 1-unit increase in x.

quiz.q: Using ŷ = 3x + 10, predict y when x = 5
Which best describes a residual?
o: The slope of the regression line
quiz.e: A residual measures how far off a prediction was from the actual data point.

quiz.q: Two variables have r = 0.91. What can you conclude?
o: They have a strong positive linear relationship, but not necessarily causation
One variable definitely causes the other
quiz.e: A strong r shows correlation, not proof of causation.

quiz.q: Predicting a value using x far beyond the range of the collected data is risky because:
o: It is extrapolation, which is less reliable
Correlation coefficients don't apply outside the data
quiz.e: Extrapolating beyond the observed data range reduces prediction reliability.

quiz.q: If f(x) = 5x − 2, find f(0)
If f(x) = x² + 4, find f(−3)
What is the domain of f(x) = 3/(x+5)?
quiz.e: The denominator cannot be zero, so x ≠ −5.

quiz.q: A relation contains (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), (1,8). Is this a function?
o: No, x=1 has two different outputs
quiz.e: x=1 maps to both 2 and 8, which violates the definition of a function.

quiz.q: The graph of g(x) = f(x) − 4 compared to f(x) is:
quiz.e: Subtracting outside the function shifts the graph down.

quiz.q: Which relation passes the Vertical Line Test?
quiz.e: y=x² is a function — every vertical line crosses it exactly once. The others fail the test.

quiz.q: Find the average rate of change of f(x) = 2x + 3 between x=1 and x=4
quiz.e: For a linear function, average rate of change always equals the slope: 2.

PART_B1.q: Write the equation of a line with slope −4 through (0, −3)
PART_B1.e: y = mx + b with m = −4 and b = −3 (the given y-intercept).

PART_B1.q: How many solutions does the system 2x + y = 6 and 4x + 2y = 12 have?
PART_B1.e: Dividing the second equation by 2 gives 2x + y = 6 — the exact same line.
Distribute both terms and combine like terms to get x³ + x² − 7x + 2.

PART_B1.q: How many real solutions does 2x² − 3x + 5 = 0 have?
PART_B1.e: Discriminant = (−3)² − 4(2)(5) = 9 − 40 = −31, which is negative — no real solutions.

PART_B1.q: A bacteria culture of 200 doubles every hour. Which equation models the population after t hours?
PART_B1.e: Doubling is a growth factor of 2 applied t times: y = 200(2)ᵗ.

PART_B2.q: A data set has the five-number summary: min=4, Q1=10, median=14, Q3=20, max=30. Find the IQR and explain what it represents.
PART_B2.sa: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 20 − 10 = 10. It represents the range of the middle 50% of the data, and unlike the full range, it is resistant to outliers.

PART_B2.q: Explain why a strong correlation coefficient does not prove causation. Give an example.
PART_B2.sa: A strong correlation only shows that two variables tend to change together, not that one causes the other. For example, ice cream sales and drowning rates are strongly correlated, but both are actually caused by a third variable — hot summer weather — not by each other.

PART_B2.q: Solve the compound inequality −2 ≤ 3x + 1 ≤ 10 and describe the solution set.
PART_B2.sa: Subtract 1 from all three parts: −3 ≤ 3x ≤ 9. Divide by 3: −1 ≤ x ≤ 3. The solution is all x between −1 and 3, inclusive.

PART_B2.q: Explain, using the Vertical Line Test, why the graph of a circle is not a function.
PART_B2.sa: A circle fails the Vertical Line Test because a vertical line drawn through the middle of the circle crosses the graph at two points, one above the center and one below. Since one x-value would correspond to two different y-values, the circle is not a function.

PART_C.q: A line passes through (2, 5) and is parallel to the line y = 3x − 4. Write the equation of this new line in slope-intercept form, showing all work.
PART_C.sa: Parallel lines have the same slope, so m = 3. Using point-slope form: y − 5 = 3(x − 2) → y − 5 = 3x − 6 → y = 3x − 1.

PART_C.q: Solve x² − 4x − 5 = 0 using the quadratic formula. Show all substitution and simplification steps.

A savings account starts with $1,000 and earns 4% interest per year, compounded annually. Write an equation for the account balance after t years, and find the balance after 5 years, rounded to the nearest dollar.
Factor 2x² + 5x − 3 completely, then use the factored form to solve 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0.
PART_C.sa: 2x² + 5x − 3 = (2x − 1)(x + 3). Setting each factor to 0: 2x − 1 = 0 → x = 1/2, or x + 3 = 0 → x = −3.
